items.descriptionOriginal: For generations, a story about two tigers has travelled through Gond households in Madhya Pradesh's Kanha landscape. They were called Ram and Laxman. According to the oral tradition remembered by Dayal Singh Kusre, a Gond Adivasi who worked as a cook in different parts of Kanha, the tigers once shared a household with people. People fed them, treated them with respect, and regarded them as protectors. The story survives in community memory, along with a practice of making offerings to tigers. It is not a scientific account of tiger behaviour. For Kusre, the story is inseparable from a larger understanding of nature. "Forests and wildlife are not something to be protected from a distance. Both are part of a shared landscape, where people must learn how to live alongside other species", Kusre tells The Better India. But can cultural memory really help people negotiate their place alongside wild animals? When tigers were part of the household Kusre recalls a Gond tribal story in which Ram and Laxman occupied a place within the household's collective memory. According to the Gond folklore, family members were instructed not to encounter the tigers when they first entered the household. A newly married bride, in particular, was told not to open a particular locked room or door. Tigers are elusive, and their presence in a landscape does not necessarily mean that people regularly see them. Photograph: (Videograb-The Corbett Foundation; Dasra India) The restriction was associated with the belief that the tigers would not recognise a new family member, much as traditional households have sometimes maintained rules around interactions between younger women and senior male relatives. In the story, one daughter-in-law eventually opened the door without knowing or following the instructions. She saw the tiger's face, and the animal left the household. Kusre recounts the tiger's message to the family's eldest man: he would now stay in the forest and receive his food there. The room and its closed door represent a boundary that members of the household were expected to respect. The tiger was part of the story, but so was the responsibility of people to recognise that a relationship with wildlife came with limits. The tradition also carries an idea of reciprocity. Kusre says, "The family believed that if people had food, they should ensure that the wildlife around them was fed, too" He also describes a practice of making an offering of a goat or a hen to the tiger in the forest once a year, with the belief that the animal would continue to protect the family. 'Nature is our all' For Kusre, reverence for Ram and Laxman is part of a wider relationship with nature. "For us, nature is our all; we bow at her feet," he says. "If we have to cross 10 km of forests also, then we pray to nature, and the Adivasis feel confident. They trust nature for protection." He also recalls what he describes as older Gond beliefs about encounters with tigers. "Our ancestors used to cross paths with tigers normally, but in reality, tiger spotting is difficult," he says. Tigers are elusive, and their presence in a landscape does not necessarily mean that people regularly see them. These details belong to Kusre's account of Gond oral tradition , but it does not suggest that people should approach, feed, or attempt to house wild tigers today. The meanings communities attach to an animal can also influence whether its continued presence is regarded as valuable. Photograph: (The Corbett Foundation; Dasra India) Its relevance lies in what the narrative reveals about the values through which tribal communities understand the natural world. What communities learn from living alongside wildlife Conservation biologist Shivangi Bendre, whose work focuses primarily on the Central Indian landscape, and mitigating human-wildlife conflict, says it is important to understand the everyday practices through which communities adapt to the presence of wild animals. "I think it is important to look not just at the living practices of communities, but also at their livelihoods and the different, sometimes ingenious, ways they have developed to live alongside wildlife. These practices emerge from generations of experience of sharing landscapes with wild animals," she tells The Better India. Bendre points to communities living alongside sloth bears in Hampi as an example. Drawing insights from Wildlife Conservation Society India's report "A relational perspective of Sloth Bear - Human Relations in Hampi region of Karnataka" by Mohammed Hisham K, she says, 'when sloth bears enter an area, people may light fires, clap or make sounds to alert the animals to their presence." "The idea is to communicate, in a way the animals can recognise, that people are present . Rather than reacting when an encounter happens, community members use these practices to signal their presence and reduce the likelihood of a surprise encounter," she explains. These practices or stories should not automatically be treated as universally effective or safe. Their usefulness depends on the species, local conditions, and the circumstances of an encounter. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Harsha Tej | Lake Conservation, Planting Trees & Farming 🌍 (@muddyfingerss) Still, Bendre says that the knowledge developed by people who live alongside wildlife deserves consideration in conservation planning. Their experiences can help researchers understand how encounters happen, what people fear and which locally developed responses may help reduce risks. When a feared animal becomes part of culture Bendre also points to Pilivesha, a traditional tiger dance practised in Karnataka, as an example of how cultural expression can shape the way people relate to wildlife. In Pilivesha, performers portray tigers through dance and elaborate body painting. The animal becomes part of a public cultural expression, represented through movement, performance and artistic skill. "What is interesting is how such cultural practices can shape the way people relate to an animal that might otherwise evoke fear," Bendre says. In the context she describes, the tradition has helped make the tiger more familiar as a cultural symbol, with some reduction in the fear associated with its presence. Research by Rohan Sharma of WCS India, " Celebrating Nature-Culture Relationships: Documenting Cultures and Traditions of Tiger Folklore in Coastal Karnataka through the Annual Pilivesha Celebrations" , also offers context to this relationship. The research explores how the tradition does not mean that it necessarily reduces conflict with wild tigers, or that cultural familiarity can substitute for practical safety measures. It shows how an animal's place in community life can extend beyond the risks associated with encounters. Dikesh Chaudhary, project officer at The Corbett Foundation, stresses the importance of preserving such traditions as part of community history. "The idea is to save the tradition. It is a challenge, the cultural part. It is part of the history of the Gond and Baiga communities, and it is thus important," he says. For Chaudhary, these traditions also offer a response to a question that can arise in conservation discussions: why should tigers be protected? "There are people who still may have questions: 'Baagh kyun bachana hai?' (Why should we save the tiger? This is the answer to that question. We should know why we need to save the tiger." Communities need reliable information about animal behaviour, practical guidance on reducing encounters and access to appropriate support when incidents occur. Photograph: (Apoorva Jadon) Cultural traditions cannot, on their own, explain every ecological reason for conserving a species. Tigers play a role in forest ecosystems, and their protection is connected to the wider conservation of habitats and biodiversity. But the meanings communities attach to an animal can also influence whether its continued presence is regarded as valuable. Are all traditional beliefs good for conservation? Respecting cultural memory does not mean accepting every traditional belief without question. Some beliefs may discourage the killing of animals or encourage people to regard wildlife as worthy of protection. Others may have little direct bearing on conservation. And some can create risks for people, particularly when a belief influences decisions during a medical emergency. Where wildlife-related risks affect livelihoods or safety, conservation efforts must also take those everyday realities seriously. Photograph: (Sangeetha Balaji) Bendre talks about this distinction through an example she encountered in studies in Kanha, where a belief about snakebite can influence how people respond after being bitten. "The belief is that there's this one particular jari-booti(medicinal herb) that, when the person who's been bitten consumes it, the snake, wherever it is, will die and split into two halves," she says. According to Bendre, people who believe in this remedy may turn to traditional healers rather than take the person who has been bitten to a hospital. The problem, she explains, is not that the belief exists. It is that following it may delay treatment and put the person's life at risk. "They're not really directly attacking the snake, but at the same time, that superstition may cause the person's life to be in danger," she says. A belief that does not directly encourage people to kill a snake may have a different conservation implication from one that delays potentially life-saving medical care. The question, therefore, is not whether traditional beliefs should be accepted or rejected wholesale. It is how to recognise their significance while addressing practices that create risks. Awareness is only part of the answer "Education and awareness and primary healthcare is also something that needs to be addressed in parallel with whatever awareness that we do on the conservation front," Bendre says. Communities need reliable information about animal behaviour, practical guidance on reducing encounters and access to appropriate support when incidents occur. Where wildlife-related risks affect livelihoods or safety, conservation efforts must also take those everyday realities seriously. The story of Ram and Laxman cannot tell us how tigers behave, whether they recognise people as family or whether feeding an animal will make it a protector. Those questions require evidence, and the story should not be treated as a guide to interacting with wild tigers. In Kusre's telling, the tigers' departure from the household does not end the relationship. The story continues through remembrance, reverence, and the belief that the forest remains their place. Its central idea is not that wild animals should live with people, but that people must recognise their place in a landscape they share with other species. Coexistence does not mean eliminating every boundary between humans and wildlife. It means finding ways to live alongside animals while respecting their ecological needs and protecting human lives.

items.descriptionOriginal: A garden in the middle of a city can be more than a patch of green. Look closely, and you might spot a butterfly moving between flowers, bees hovering over native plants, and children exploring the outdoors at their own pace. These small encounters are part of a much bigger story about biodiversity, belonging and the spaces we make for nature. In Ludhiana, Punjab, 16-year-old Gunisha Kaur is helping bring this vision to life. Through her initiative, Buzzing Blooms, she has established more than 20 pollinator gardens and ecological restoration projects across Ludhiana, Meerut, Mumbai and partner communities. Through Buzzing Blooms, Gunisha is transforming underused urban spaces into chemical-free habitats for bees, butterflies and other pollinators. Photograph: ( Buzzing Blooms ) Her work has now earned her third place at the 2026 International Young Eco-Hero Awards , presented by environmental organisation Action For Nature. Over 24 months of monitoring, the gardens recorded a 155% increase in pollinator species richness, from 18 species to 46. Bee visits also increased by nearly 200%, according to the organisation. But for Gunisha, the idea was never just about planting more flowers. It was also about creating outdoor spaces where people with different needs could feel comfortable and connected to nature. How a personal experience inspired Buzzing Blooms Growing up in Ludhiana, an industrialised city, Gunisha became concerned about the declining pollinator populations she observed around her. At the same time, her experiences at home were shaping how she understood the relationship between people and the natural world. Watching her younger autistic brother helped her recognise how calming natural surroundings could be. It also made her aware of how few outdoor spaces were designed to accommodate neurodivergent children and their sensory needs. The gardens feature native plants, structured pathways and touch-safe greenery to make nature more accessible to children with different sensory needs. Photograph: (Instagram/ @ gunisha_eco ) These observations led her to launch Buzzing Blooms on 5 March 2023, with a vision to transform underused urban spaces into chemical-free habitats that support both biodiversity and inclusion. Her Sikh heritage, which emphasises respect for nature, also informs her approach. "Rooted in my culture, which teaches respect for nature, I was inspired to create spaces that nurture both biodiversity and belonging," she adds. Gardens designed for bees, butterflies and children At Buzzing Blooms, the idea of a successful garden extends beyond how it looks. The spaces use layers of native plants and chemical-free cultivation methods to create habitats for pollinators, including bees and butterflies. The design also considers the people who visit. Structured pathways make the gardens easier to navigate, while non-thorny, touch-safe plants and designated bee- and butterfly-watching zones allow children to explore nature in ways that suit their sensory needs. The result is an approach that brings ecological restoration and accessibility together, rather than treating them as separate goals. Over 24 months of monitoring, Buzzing Blooms recorded a 155% increase in pollinator species richness, from 18 to 46 species. Photograph: ( Buzzing Blooms ) And the impact goes beyond the gardens themselves. Buzzing Blooms has engaged more than 4,000 students, including over 250 neurodivergent and vulnerable individuals. Through workshops, restoration drives and inclusive learning programmes, the initiative has reached more than 8,000 people. Gunisha has also established the Buzzing Blooms Peer Advocacy Network, training more than 500 young ambassadors in environmental communication, public speaking and leadership. To help fund the work, she conducts art classes on weekends and reinvests her earnings, alongside money from plant sales and scholarships, into maintaining the gardens. From local gardens to international recognition Gunisha's interest in finding solutions to environmental challenges also extends to technology. She developed AeroBloom, an artificial-intelligence-guided aerial pollination system designed to support agriculture during extreme heat, when natural pollinators may temporarily leave an area. The innovation earned her a bronze medal at the Indian Science and Engineering Fair. Gunisha Kaur wins third place at the 2026 International Young Eco-Hero Awards for her work with Buzzing Blooms. Photograph: ( Buzzing Blooms ) Her latest recognition at the International Young Eco-Hero Awards puts a spotlight on what a young changemaker can achieve by addressing environmental problems within her own community. From creating habitats for pollinators to making green spaces more welcoming for children, Gunisha's work offers a practical lesson in how cities can become more inclusive while supporting biodiversity. Sources: 'Meet Gunisha Kaur, the 16-year-old from Ludhiana who won third place at the 2026 Internation Young Eco Awards' by The Times Of India, Published ob 16 October 2026. 'Gunisha Kaur' Action For Nature. items.descriptionOriginal: For 39 years, Marilyn Hampton swept floors, bought supplies for children who couldn't afford them, and turned smiles "up instead of down" -- work she once measured against a college degree she never earned and found herself wanting. The custodian who privately carried a sense of failure was, to everyone around her, the living heart of Aubrey Independent School District in Texas. When the superintendent called her to the podium under the pretense of a routine meeting, Hampton unrolled a small red carpet and found her own name printed on it: Marilyn Hampton Elementary School. The next day, she was still crying. "Whoever thought a janitor would have a school named after them," she said, and in that sentence lives the quiet revelation the story holds: that a life spent in faithful, unglamorous service to others can quietly become the most significant thing in a room, in a district, in a community's memory -- long before anyone thinks to say so out loud.

items.descriptionOriginal: "We didn't know if we had enough money to complete the journey. We did not even know what we would do when we came back. But we knew that if we kept waiting for the right time, we might never go." For Samrat Ulhas Dambe (30) and his wife Varshali Samrat Dambe (35) losing their jobs in 2024 brought an uncertain future into focus. Both had worked in the corporate world, building careers and following familiar routines . Then, around June that year, they were laid off. With a few months ahead of them and no solid idea of what came next, they began thinking about a dream they had carried for years. Could they ride along India's borders on their motorcycle? The idea had been with Samrat since he was 12, when he would draw the outline of India and imagine tracing its borders on a bike. Over the years, it became a dream the couple shared. They had been riding together since 2018 and bought a Benelli TRK in 2022, hoping to take on longer adventures. Now, with time on their hands but limited savings, they decided to attempt the journey, which they called the 'Art India Ride'. On 19 September 2024, they left their home in Mhapral, a village in Maharashtra's Ratnagiri district, about 150 kilometres from Mumbai. They would spend the next 80 days travelling 16,428 km, covering 22 states and four Union Territories, through deserts, mountain passes, remote border settlements, and unfamiliar roads. They returned home on 8 December 2024, having completed a journey they had once thought they might only manage halfway. In January 2025, their achievement was recognised by the India Book of Records as IBR Achiever 2025. But the record was only one part of the story. Along the way, the couple faced freezing temperatures, tight budgets, and moments when they wondered whether they should turn back. They also found strangers who welcomed them into their homes, fed them, and treated them like family. When the time finally felt right Before the journey, Samrat worked as a digital marketing expert at a multinational company, while Varshali was a digital marketing manager at a digital agency. Their lives revolved around work and the usual plans people make for the future. They had been riding together since 2018 and bought a Benelli TRK in 2022, hoping to take on longer adventures. The layoffs in June 2024 left them with uncertainty, but also something they rarely had before. Time. "We suddenly had three to four months available, and we didn't know exactly what we were going to do next," the husband tells The Better India . "It was an uncertain phase, but we began to see it as an opportunity to do something we had always wanted to do." Samrat's dream of riding around India's borders had never really gone away. The couple had already spent years riding together, and the idea of taking on the country's outer reaches felt like a natural next step. By August, they had decided to go ahead. They did not have enough savings to be certain they could complete the whole route. At first, they thought they might travel through only half of India. Still, they did not want to keep postponing the dream until their finances were more comfortable. "If we waited for the perfect financial moment, we knew life would get in the way, and the dream might fade. We decided to start and see how far our resources would take us," Varshali adds. There was one last change before departure. They had initially planned to travel south first, but heavy rainfall across South India prompted them to rethink the route. With just eight days to go, they decided to begin in Gujarat and travel clockwise around the country instead. On 19 September, they set off from Mhapral, carrying excitement, nervousness, and no guarantee of how far they would get. Five bags and a budget to stretch The couple knew that completing the journey would require careful spending. Their Benelli TRK averaged around 20 km per litre, so fuel was a major expense. They set a daily limit of Rs 3,500 for fuel, food and accommodation, and generally looked for rooms costing no more than Rs 1,000 to Rs 1,500 a night. They ate at small local eateries and kept their stays simple. The couple had no elaborate itinerary mapping out every day. Instead, they usually decided their next halt and route only a day or two in advance. "We wanted to remain flexible. Weather, road conditions and accommodation could change our plans at any time," she explains. That flexibility had already proved useful when they changed their route before setting off. It also gave them the freedom to travel places they had not known much about before reaching them. Packing was another exercise in deciding what they could do without. For 80 days, their belongings fitted into five bags. Each had a saddlebag for clothes and personal items. A top box carried their laptop, cameras, electronic equipment, and a basic toolkit. Their tank bag held phones, documents and essentials, while an additional bag carried winter layers and raincoats. They travelled with just three T-shirts, two pairs of jeans and their riding gear, along with the equipment they needed for the road. "Travelling with so little taught us that we didn't need as many things as we thought we did," Samrat says. Their money was always part of the calculation. Fuel, food, accommodation, and motorcycle maintenance all had to fit within their means. They had also agreed that if their savings fell to Rs 40,000, they would return home and look for jobs. That possibility meant every stretch of road carried a question . Could they afford to keep going? Would the weather cooperate? Where would they sleep that night? Now, with time on their hands but limited savings, they decided to attempt the journey, which they called the 'Art India Ride'. They decided to continue riding, figuring out the road ahead as they went. The road tested them before it rewarded them Their route took them from Maharashtra through Gujarat and Rajasthan, then Haryana and Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh. They continued through Chandigarh, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, before reaching West Bengal and Sikkim. From there, they rode through Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Meghalaya, then followed the eastern coast through Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. After reaching Kanyakumari, they turned back north through Kerala, Karnataka and Goa, completing their journey in Maharashtra. The first few days were harder than they had imagined. Near Santalpur, around the Gujarat-Rajasthan border, they crossed a long, isolated stretch without seeing another person. A storm rolled in, the power went out, and the area began to feel unfamiliar. The only hotel they could find was surrounded by parked trucks, with only truck drivers stopping there for the night. Samrat grew anxious and began wondering whether they should turn back. Varshali encouraged him to continue. It was a difficult moment, not because the couple had suddenly stopped believing in their dream, but because they were realising what it meant to pursue it without knowing what lay ahead. Ladakh brought another set of challenges. They reached the high-altitude region in October, when the tourist season was winding down, and many hotels had closed. Around Pangong Lake, temperatures dropped to minus 12 degrees Celsius. They had not ridden in Ladakh before and had not fully anticipated how harsh the conditions could be. Poor network connectivity, difficult roads and the remoteness of some stretches added to their worries. They were also concerned about getting a puncture on their motorcycle's tube tyres in places where help could be difficult to find. At Upshi, the cold became particularly difficult for Varshali, who was shivering. They eventually found a local Maharashtrian who helped them arrange a room with a heater. The experience taught them to adjust quickly, look out for each other and accept help when they needed it. There were no guarantees that the next day would be easier, but they learnt to deal with one challenge at a time. The strangers who made them feel at home For the couple, the most memorable parts of the journey were the people they met rather than the places they saw. In Punjab, a family welcomed them into their home and insisted they stay as guests. In Tawang, Arunachal Pradesh, a woman from Maharashtra who lived there offered them prayers and blessings for the road ahead, greeting them with a traditional Tibetan white shawl. In Bhalukpong, they met an elderly couple who ran a cafe. The two travellers formed a warm connection with the uncle, who treated Samrat with the affection he might show his own son. When the couple returned to see him on their way back, he became emotional as they prepared to leave. Thousands of kilometres from home, they found people willing to make space for them, share what they had and offer encouragement without expecting anything in return. Their journey also gave them a closer view of life in remote border regions and the work of the Indian Army and the Border Security Force. They came away with a stronger appreciation of the people who live in difficult conditions and those who serve in them. "Before the journey, India was a map of different states, languages, food, and cultures," the husband explains. "After travelling 16,428 kilometres, it felt like one giant, compassionate family. The warmth we received from people remained largely similar, wherever we went." One encounter in North Bengal brought home just how far a journey can reach beyond the people making it. Travelling from Sikkim towards Jaigaon in West Bengal, the couple stopped at a small stall for breakfast. A group of people arrived by car and noticed the Maharashtra registration on their motorcycle. Curious about how far they had travelled, they invited the couple to sit with them and talk. The conversation lasted nearly two hours. One of the men, Arun Sircar, a corporate professional from Kolkata, explained why he had been asking so many questions. "Once upon a time, this was my dream too. I moved to the USA, worked hard, and bought a luxury BMW because I wanted to travel. My wife and I wanted to live life on the road, just like you. But somehow, life caught up with us, and we got stuck," he says. He had driven across the United States but had never experienced his own country in the way the couple was doing. "You are living my dream, bro. Through your journey, I feel like I am travelling too," he told them. The couple knew that completing the journey would require careful spending. The words moved Samrat and Varshali. Their ride had begun as a personal ambition , but here was someone who felt connected to it because it represented a life he had once imagined for himself. Sircar and his wife invited the couple to their home. She prepared a vegetarian feast despite not having cooked vegetarian food before, and they invited friends over to hear about the journey. The couple were also given a room for the night. For the travelling duo, the connection became a reminder that a journey could mean something to people who had never taken the same road themselves. What the road taught them Kaushal Sethia, a 26-year-old software engineer from Surat, had met the couple in Naggar, Himachal Pradesh, where they were neighbours at a homestay. They spent almost a month together and became close friends. When the duo began their border expedition, Sethia and his family followed their progress and regularly asked for updates. What stayed with him was not just the distance they covered. "The way they support each other is what makes the journey special. It tests you physically, mentally, and emotionally. The most difficult part of a journey is starting, and they didn't just start it. They completed it against all the problems," he says. The 80 days had tested the couple's relationship, too. Sharing a motorcycle, limited belongings and constant uncertainty meant making decisions together, managing tiredness and adapting to changing conditions. They learnt to recognise when one of them needed encouragement, rest or a little space. For Samrat, riding also became a way of silencing the noise in his head. "When you are on a motorcycle for days at a time, the beat of the engine and the focus the road demands bring you into the present moment," he says. "For me, it feels like meditation." The couple returned to Mhapral on 8 December 2024, after spending 80 days on the road. Their total expenditure came to around Rs 3.75 lakh, covering fuel, food, accommodation, repairs, and maintenance. They had completed the journey without knowing at the outset whether their savings would last. They had also returned with memories of people who had made the road feel less lonely. They were not thinking about a record while travelling. After reaching Goa, a friend suggested that they apply to the India Book of Records. They submitted photographs, fuel receipts, and other documents for verification, and in January 2025, they were recognised as IBR Achiever 2025. The recognition was welcome, but the couple say the people they met and what they learnt mattered more than the certificate. Their route took them from Maharashtra through Gujarat and Rajasthan, then Haryana and Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh. Carrying the journey forward On 6 April 2025, Samrat and Varshali started 'Souls of Motorcycle', a riding community inspired by what the Art India Ride had taught them. They wanted to create a space for motorcycle enthusiasts to learn, travel responsibly and experience the road as more than a test of speed, distance or engine capacity. The community has grown to more than 700 members, with over 8,000 Instagram followers. The couple organise rides to destinations such as Ladakh and Sikkim and are working to expand into cities including Surat, Chandigarh, Kolkata, and Bengaluru. Their aim is to help more people become confident riders, discover places they might not otherwise visit and find some mental space away from their everyday routines. For the couple, riding is not only about reaching a destination. It is also about being present, meeting people and returning with a different perspective on life. The Art India Ride gave them a way to experience that for themselves, and Souls of Motorcycle is how they now hope to share it with others. Their journey began at a moment when the future felt uncertain. They had lost their jobs, their savings were limited and they could not be sure they would complete the route. But rather than waiting for life to become predictable, they chose to begin. They rode through freezing nights and lonely stretches, accepted help from strangers and experienced how much could happen when two people kept moving towards the same goal. The record gave their journey a number. The people they met gave it meaning. And the dream that began with a boy drawing the outline of India became 16,428 kilometres of road, shared courage, and a reminder that sometimes the right time is the time you decide to start. All pictures courtesy Varshali Dambe.

items.title: Τι κάνει τη Scary Music Scary; Ο συνθέτης "Obsession" για τη δημιουργία μιας ταινίας τρόμου δολοφονίας
items.titleOriginal: What Makes Scary Music Scary? The “Obsession” Composer on Crafting a Killer Horror Movie Score
items.description: Στο δεύτερο μισό της ταινίας The Shining του Stanley Kubrick, υπάρχει μια εμβληματική σεκάνς που είναι αναμφισβήτητα τόσο τρομακτική όσο η έξαψη με τσεκούρι του Jack Nicholson. Ξεκινά ήσυχα, η κάμερα ακολουθεί τη Shelley Duvall καθώς περπατά προς ένα σκιερό δωμάτιο. Τα βήματά της αντηχούν στη σιωπή προτού εισέλθει ένας δυσοίωνος ήχος, σχεδόν σαν παραμορφωμένος λευκός θόρυβος. Ο…
items.descriptionOriginal: In the second half of Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining , there’s an iconic sequence that’s arguably as terrifying as Jack Nicholson’s ax-wielding rampage. It begins quietly, the camera following Shelley Duvall as she walks toward a shadowy room. Her footsteps echo in the silence before an ominous sound creeps in, almost like distorted white noise. The music builds, getting louder and more complex as warped high notes slowly penetrate the din. It’s chaotic, dissonant, deafening, mirroring the emotions on Duvall’s face, until finally, finally — well, we won’t give you any spoilers . “If you watched it on mute, I don’t know if it would feel nearly as scary,” Rock Burwell told Nice News of the classic flick. Burwell composed the score for this year’s breakout indie horror film, Obsession , which raked in $500 million-plus off a $750,000 budget, making it the highest-grossing movie ever produced for under $1 million. The Los Angeles-based composer recognizes how essential music is to evoking emotion in filmgoers, and his eerie orchestration played an outsize role in Obsession’s success. “What just generally has always drawn me to music in the first place is its ability to influence how we feel,” he said. But what exactly makes scary music scary? We may all have some general idea of the characteristics of creepy music — the crescendo of staccato strings in Psycho ’s shower scene comes to mind — but the way in which a score achieves its effect varies greatly. There are certain common elements, however, that lend themselves to disconcerting an audience. Subverting Expectations For Obsession , Burwell — after discussions with writer-director Curry Barker — chose a nontraditional approach, opting to subtly discomfit viewers through dreamy, nostalgic melodies, slightly pitch-bending his notes and drenching everything in reverb. “It was fun to explore not coming in with these really harsh, interval, screechy-sounding kind of things that you hear in a lot of horror movies,” he explained, “but actually coming from something that feels a bit more warm and almost comforting. But the way it moves and is undulating underneath is very — it kind of gets under your skin a little bit more.” Composer Katy Jarzebowski , who recently scored the award-winning documentary Gaslit featuring Jane Fonda, has been working in the industry for over 20 years. She noted that today’s savvy audiences are well-versed in the language of film. The key to unsettling them, then, is to present a musical choice they don’t necessarily understand or expect. “If you give them something that they know and love, then it kind of takes that feeling of discomfort away,” she explained, adding: “[When filmmakers] don’t give them something that they expect, it becomes uncomfortable.” Tension Tension is the heart of any horror film, and a good one typically leaves viewers on tenterhooks throughout. To that end, Burwell noted that the descending melodies and drawn-out cues he used can cause audiences to feel as though they’re suspended, waiting for a resolution that never comes. “Everything is very, like, ambient and long, and it’s slow moving,” he said. “I think that the pace of it really allows those feelings to sit in a bit longer.” He added that he’s heard from fans that the sweet-yet-tainted score had them feeling “very comforted, but at the same time, feeling kind of bad or that there’s something missing or that there’s yearning.” Jarzebowski agreed with the idea of holding out on viewers. “It’s a lot about where you choose to come in or where you choose to hold back,” she said. “You know, a lot of times [it’s] not giving that kind of pillow for the audience to land on to remind them that they’re in a movie in the first place.” In the Studio Pete Horner is an Emmy-winning sound designer and re-recording mixer at Skywalker Sound (who also happens to be married to Jarzebowski). He pointed out that the terror conveyed through a horror movie’s sound isn’t merely from the music itself. Foley is the art of creating sound effects in a studio — things like footsteps or a door creaking — and Horner said it can be used to great effect for inducing fear in quiet scenes. “By accentuating those things, it kind of draws you closer to the action, and it makes you feel uncomfortable because you shouldn’t be able to hear that,” he explained, adding: “It mimics what happens when you are scared, which is that you become hyperaware of your surroundings. And when you’re not scared, you probably don’t hear the footsteps at all, even though they are happening in the space you’re in. But if you are scared, every little tiny sound has huge meaning.” Additionally, gradually removing the ambient background noise (called “room tone”) from a scene can be extremely disconcerting. “It’s something you want to use sparingly in a movie, but if you pull out of all of the ambiences, the effect that it has is the audience will hold their breath,” Horner said. “Because they’re listening, they’re trying to hear into the sound, and there’s nothing there. And it’s a very scary feeling.” Working With the Cinematography It’s typical for musicians to score to picture, meaning they create the music as they watch the film. But sometimes, the two arts inform each other more equally. In Obsession , Burwell sent early cues to Barker while he and director of photography Taylor Clemons were coming up with the shot list. Barker later told Burwell that playing the music on set really helped establish the mood they were going for. Likewise, watching Clemons’ claustrophobic cinematography influenced Burwell’s choices for the score. “We kind of leaned on the darkness, like, there’s not much high frequency information in the music, and there’s not a whole lot of light in a lot of these scenes, too,” Burwell said. “I’ve kind of referred to it as a lot of the score feeling like a lead blanket or something like that. Like, it’s just really heavy. And I think the cinematography really informed that for me.” Experimentation Starting with what’s considered the first-ever horror flick (a three-minute silent French film from 1896 titled The Haunted Castle ) to the dozens coming out in 2027 , the genre is a confirmed favorite of moviegoers. Call it sublimation or call it masochism, but people like to be scared. And that means composers have ample opportunity — and one could say the imperative — to get creative. “Horror is a great place for composers, especially to experiment with different things because a lot of times, you’re trying to create a fear that someone doesn’t know yet,” Jarzebowski said, adding: “We already have Psycho , we have Stranger Things , we have [horror filmmaker and composer John] Carpenter — all this horror language that we’ve created. So you already know what to be scared of. So there’s always room for, like, ‘OK, what else can we do to make it even scarier? What haven’t they heard yet?’”

items.description: Τι σε τρομάζει; Ένας μυστηριώδης γδούπος κάτω στη μέση της νύχτας, να εντοπίσεις μια αράχνη στο μαξιλάρι σου και να νιώθεις κάτι να πιέζει το πόδι σου στη θάλασσα είναι μεταξύ των 10 κορυφαίων πραγμάτων που κάνουν τους Βρετανούς να ουρλιάζουν, σύμφωνα με μια πρόσφατη έρευνα 2.000 ενηλίκων στο Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο.…
items.descriptionOriginal: What spooks you? A mysterious thud downstairs in the middle of the night, spotting a spider on your pillow, and feeling something brush against your leg in the sea are among the top 10 things that make Brits scream, according to a recent survey of 2,000 adults in the U.K. Yet despite being quick to shriek, the nation appears to embrace the fun side of fear, with 84% of respondents saying scary experiences are more likely to end in laughter than panic when shared with others. More than half also confirmed enjoying spooky thrills in a group setting tends to leave them laughing, particularly when watching horror films, riding roller coasters, or braving a haunted attraction. SWNS According to psychologist Kimberley Wilson, there’s a scientific reason these scary experiences can feel surprisingly enjoyable, something she’s dubbed the “Shared Shriek Effect.” “When we watch something scary, our bodies respond as if we’re facing a threat. Our heart rate increases, adrenaline rises, and our attention sharpens,” she told SWNS. “The difference is that our brains know we’re actually safe, which allows us to experience that physical rush as excitement rather than fear.” Wilson added: “When we share that experience with other people, whether we’re jumping, screaming, or laughing together, it can create a genuine sense of connection. The scream itself also helps release the tension that’s been building up, which is why laughter so often follows.” There are benefits beyond the thrill, too, with a quarter saying that being scared offers an escape from everyday life, while 24% see it as a healthy emotional release. Nearly 1 in 5 of those polled also believe it acts as an instant stress reliever. The research was done via OnePoll and commissioned by M&M’s to mark the launch of the candy brand’s new “ Screaming Service ,” encouraging people to swap streaming for screaming this Halloween. “We think Halloween isn’t really about being scared, it’s about screaming together,” said Georgia Woodward, a senior brand manager at M&M’s. “Our ‘Screaming Service’ celebrates those moments across the month of Halloween when everyone jumps at the same scenes, hides behind a cushion, and ends up laughing together about it afterwards.” Top 10 Things That Make Brits Shriek SWNS 1. Someone unexpectedly jumping out at you as a prank 2. Hearing a knock at the window when it’s dark 3. Hearing a mysterious thud downstairs in the night 4. Missing a step at the bottom of the stairs 5. Spotting a spider on your pillow 6. Feeling something brush against your leg in the sea 7. Seeing a mouse dart across a room 8. Being caught off guard by a spooky film twist 9. Someone unexpectedly shouting “boo!” 10. Walking face-first into a cobweb This article was originally written by Zara Zubeidi for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Can everyday dietary lecithin defend against memory loss? A study of 1,917 older adults combining MoCA assessments with targeted lipidomics reveals that lecithin and polyunsaturated phosphatidylcholine are linked to lower rates of mild cognitive impairment, particularly in adults with lower education.

Η Klebsiella pneumoniae είναι ένα επικίνδυνο βακτήριο που σκοτώνει χιλιάδες βρέφη σε χώρες χαμηλού και μεσαίου εισοδήματος κάθε χρόνο και είναι ο μεγαλύτερος δολοφόνος παιδιών παγκοσμίως. Τέτοιες λοιμώξεις μπορεί να είναι δύσκολες…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have discovered that vaccinating mouse mothers transfers antibodies that defend vulnerable newborns against Klebsiella pneumoniae . Klebsiella pneumoniae is a dangerous bacterium that kills thousands of infants in low- and middle-income countries each year and is the leading killer of children globally. Such infections can be difficult to treat due to the bacterium’s growing resistance to antibiotics and there is currently no vaccine available to prevent infection. The study in Science Advances points to a promising new strategy for protecting vulnerable infants from the drug-resistant superbug by harnessing maternal immunity. “ Klebsiella pneumoniae is a serious threat to newborns who have not yet developed their own immune defenses,” says the study’s senior author, David A. Rosen, an associate professor of pediatrics and of molecular microbiology at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. “Our study shows that maternal immunization can effectively bridge that critical window of vulnerability, giving newborns the protection they need right from birth.” K. pneumoniae is a big problem around the world, especially in the hospital where it can cause pneumonia and other infections among adults and children. In low- and middle-income countries, where children often get exposed to the bacterium in their environment, it drives severe bacterial blood infections, known as sepsis. Because K. pneumoniae is increasingly resistant to standard antibiotics, doctors are often left without effective medicines to treat such infections. The Rosen team collaborated with the lab of Drew Schwartz, an assistant professor of pediatrics, to model K. pneumoniae sepsis in newborn mice that mimics the infection seen in children and asked if vaccinating a pregnant mouse would prevent infection in pups. Female mice were immunized at the time of mating and then again once or twice during pregnancy. The vaccine targets two of the most dangerous types of K. pneumoniae —known as K1 and K2—and was developed by Omniose, a St. Louis-based startup. Rosen had previously published findings that show the vaccine is effective in preventing K. pneumoniae infection in adult mice that can progress to life-threatening liver, respiratory tract, bloodstream, and other infections. Two weeks after birth, the young mice were exposed to lethal doses of the bacteria, either the K1 or K2 type. Of the two-week-old mouse pups from unvaccinated mothers, 0% infected with the K1 type and less than 35% with the K2 type survived. In contrast, of the young mice from vaccinated mothers, more than 80% infected with either type survived. Whether the mother received two or three doses of the vaccine did not impact survival. The researchers drew blood weekly from the young mice starting on their day of birth and continuing up to six weeks of life. They also collected breast milk from lactating mice. They found high concentrations of vaccine-specific antibodies in both the milk of vaccinated mothers and their newborn mice over the course of the study. “Mice that were never immunized themselves are highly protected from a lethal infection just from the durable antibodies transferred to them from their mother,” explains first author Paeton Wantuch, a staff scientist in the Rosen lab. The researchers are now testing updated vaccines designed to shield against multiple strains of the superbug found across the globe. “This study presents the first evidence that giving moms a vaccine could be an effective strategy for protecting their babies against these severe infections,” says Rosen. “And it also has established a practical model that we can now use to test therapies and vaccines that will bring us one step closer to human clinical trials with the ultimate goal of impacting global health.” This work was supported by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Gates Foundation, and the Washington University Department of Pediatrics. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official view of the NIH, the Gates Foundation or other funders. Competing Interest Statement: Robinson LS, Darwech I, Knoot CJ, and Harding CM have a financial stake in Omniose, a for-profit entity developing bioconjugate vaccines using patented technology reflected in the data presented in this and other published manuscripts. Source: Washington University in St. Louis The post Can a vaccine for moms protect infants from a deadly superbug? appeared first on Futurity .

With all of that said and done, shall we jump into the spooky solutions of the week? Let’s get into it. Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician Karissa: The first solution is “Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician”. This piece is informed by an actual pediatrician about how to make Halloween work for every kid in your family, and the framing is really specific to each age group in a way that’s genuinely useful. For toddlers, one tip that I thought stood out was to bring a wagon, even if your kid insists they don’t need one when you’re trick-or-treating or attending some kind of Halloween event. For school-aged kids, uh, Dr. Kristen Cook, who is the pediatrician that gives all this advice in the article, frames Halloween as giving earned independence when you’re trick-or-treating, so you can, you know, hang back a couple houses, let the kids lead, but keep them in sight. And then when it comes to teenagers, they might be going to Halloween parties, and at these parties they can come across some peer pressuring situations. It’s good to talk to them about an exit plan for situations they might not be comfortable with and discuss how to deal with these potentially uncomfortable situations, but ultimately trusting them to handle it the right way. So lots of good tips here. This just brings so much Halloween nostalgia back for me. Arielle: Yeah, I, um… my parents didn’t let me participate in Halloween growing up. I know. Heartbreak. I think it just was, uh, you know, we are an immigrant family coming from a very Christian country- Yes, yeah … and they kind of saw it as, like, kind of like devil worship. But, you know, we got over that stage. I was already, um… I kinda aged out of Halloween, uh, in the traditional sense where you go trick-or-treating and all of that. But my youngest sister was able to participate, and she had, like, really fun costumes. As a little kid, she wanted to be a tissue box one year. Um- That’s a good one … which was really weird. It was, like, a High School Musical tissue box, because we had like, High School Musical, um, wrapping paper. And so that’s how she decided to dress up. Karissa: I love it. Arielle: Yeah, so I have vicarious Halloween memories through my youngest sister. Karissa: Well, I mean, as an adult now, maybe you can do some, some of this stuff. NYC food pantries are stocking pet food for struggling households Karissa: The next solution is very heartwarming, and it’s that “New York City food pantries are now stocking pet food for struggling households”. New York State just put $500,000 towards making sure pet owners don’t have to choose between feeding themselves and feeding their animals. There are now 22 food pantries across all five boroughs stocking free pet food, and the reason this program exists is kind of heartbreaking and kind of sweet at the same time. The story mentions a woman named Cassandra in Brooklyn who sometimes eats less so her Shih Tzu doesn’t go hungry, and she’s far from alone. The demand for pet food grew after SNAP benefit cuts, which tells you a lot about just how far those cuts reach into people’s lives. Animal welfare groups have known for years that financial hardship and pet surrender are directly linked, but this program is essentially trying to catch families before they hit that wall. 5 research-backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk Karissa: The next solution is a health lifestyle related one, and it’s “Five research backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk”. Columbia University researchers ran a study trying to find the minimum effective dose of movement to counteract sitting all day. The answer was actually surprisingly specific. It’s simply five minutes of walking every 30 minutes that makes a difference. NPR actually then tested that with 20,000 of their listeners and found the exact same thing. So this article breaks down that finding plus four other fixes. Arielle, have you ever heard of this tip to walk five minutes every 30 minutes? Arielle: No, but to increase focus, I use the Pomodoro Technique, which is when you set the timer for about 20- 25 minutes and then give yourself a five-minute break. Because I work from home- Yeah … I am always kind of hunched over my laptop. So that is a trick that I use, and I do generally get up and, like, walk around the house. Um- Yeah … so I guess my body intuitively knew that this was a good thing to do, but it’s nice to have the science back it up. Karissa: The whole concept of this kind of, like, movement snack, um, short burst of activity is catching fire and a good suggestion. I guess I’ll mention one more thing about this solution, but you can check out the rest on optimistdaily.com. The whole posture section of this article talks about how the idea of sitting up straight and holding it advice is actually not correct. The actual physical therapist guidance is that your best posture is your next posture, meaning any fixed position causes strain eventually. New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries Karissa: Well, the next solution is “New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries”. NJ Transit has been installing art exhibitions at train and bus stations since 2019, and the program just expanded to its eighth location. The new show is about railroads and 250 years of American history, which is a pretty fun yet informative thing to encounter while you’re just trying to catch your train, the history about railroads. But the whole premise of this is that transit spaces are great for public art because nobody goes there expecting to see any. The encounter is accidental, which makes it different from an intentional gallery visit. I really like this, um, rise of art in public spaces, and it kind of reminds me of a solution we shared a couple months ago about how over in Warsaw they’re putting libraries in commuter stations. So if you have a little time, a layover in transportation, you can go check out the library. So I think this is a really cool kind of global trend. Arielle: And it’s really nice that the program actually pays the artists stipends because public art rarely comes with a real budget, and a lot of the time public art is like a, a mural that maybe someone painted for free or graffiti, which honestly, I’m a huge fan of graffiti. Some of the tags are really impressive, and some of them- Yeah … are just kind of silly, but they’re entertaining in their own way. Um, but that obviously doesn’t come with payment. If anything, it might come with a fine. Karissa: Right. Exactly. In this broader conversation about what public spaces are for, whether that’s a transit station, a library, park, you know, it can be a lot more than just something that people move through. Student Makers: bringing free STEM to students on three continents Karissa: Moving on to the Changemaker series, we talked more about Student Makers in this deeper dive. They are a group bringing free STEM to students on three continents. And like Arielle mentioned, this is the story that made us decide to make the entire series this year about people under 30, because young people are really just doing so many impressive things to change the world. At Student Makers, former students become the instructors. It’s often high schoolers teaching middle schoolers, and the founder’s whole argument is that it’s more relatable to have, um, you know, people who are closer in age to you to help teach things than an adult expert teaching the same material. Like we mentioned, we’ll have some of the main players behind Student Makers on the podcast in the beginning of 2027, which is crazy to even say that 2027 is around the corner. But we look forward to welcoming them on and hearing directly from them. Meet Vivian Ho: the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity Arielle: I will take over from here, Karissa, and my first solution is actually the first nominated changemaker for this series. The title- Ooh … of the article is “Meet Vivian Ho, the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity”. Most programs that distribute supplies to low-income families ask that family to identify themselves before they get anything. So basically, you have to fill out a form, you check a box, you explain your situation to someone with authority over the outcome. Vivian Ho built her nonprofit, All the Same organization, around removing that whole process. Families request what they need anonymously, and nobody has to declare themselves as someone in need to get the help they need. And she started this at just 16, which is quite impressive. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: The anonymous sign-up system is what makes this really special. Vivian’s read on situations like this was that the stigma of asking for help was keeping families from asking at all. So she just said, “Let’s get rid of that.” There’s also something within this nonprofit. There’s another, uh, initiative called the Cultural Surprises program, and it’s something I hadn’t seen before. So volunteers research the cultural background of the family they’re packing for, and handmade crafts reflecting that culture go out alongside the supply package, and it turns a resource delivery into something more like recognition, something that makes that family feel really seen. I’m not gonna get into all of the details, but I do encourage people who are interested in learning more about Vivian Ho and perhaps how to support her work to check out the article because it is really, really remarkable that she was able to do this as a teenager. Karissa: Congratulations to Vivian for being nominated by two of The Optimist Daily community members who are involved with the project as well, a nomination from her co-founder and a volunteer that she inspired to start his own project nominated Vivian. So go check that out if you wanna learn more. Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems Arielle: The next solution is titled “Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems”. Kenya just signed a $160 million deal to protect nearly 67,000 square miles of some of the most important wildlife habitat in Africa, including the Maasai Mara and Tsavo. But the interesting part isn’t just the money, it’s the structure of how that money gets released, because this isn’t a grant that arrives and then disappears. So the funding mechanism is called Project Finance for Permanence. Money flows in tied to specific government policy benchmarks, and not all the money gets, uh, given upfront, let’s say. If Kenya doesn’t hit the milestones, then those funds never get released. Tsavo holds 40% of Kenya’s elephants and 20% of its critically endangered black rhinos, and that’s just to give you an idea of what’s at stake for wildlife and geographically. Kenya committed to the global 30 by 30 target and was sitting at about 20% to 23% coverage, so this deal would largely close that gap by 2030. Will vinegar actually keep bugs out this fall? Pest experts explain what works Arielle: The next solution is titled, “Will vinegar actually keep bugs out this fall? Pest experts explain what works.” So every fall, people reach for the vinegar bottle as a first line of pest defense. They spray the windows, they spray the door frames, and then it feels like they’ve done something. But two pest control experts basically say, “You’ve done nothing.” The reason why is in this article, and there’s also one fall tip in here that’s actually kind of strange and useful. So vinegar unfortunately only kills soft-bodied insects on direct wet contact, and then once it dries, then the vinegar doesn’t really do anything against cockroaches, beetles, spiders, or ants. And researchers found negligible effects on most common household insects. What really works is, like, caulking windows and weather-stripping doors and adding door sweeps. That will actually stop bugs from getting in. Spraying is just treating the symptom and not really addressing the entry point of where all of these pests try to come in and get cozy ’cause the weather outside is getting worse. Um- Yeah … and then the, the weird tip, well, I found it weird or unexpected, is the acorn tip. If you are bringing acorns or pine cones inside this fall, then you should put them in 150-degree Fahrenheit oven for about 30 minutes first, and that will kill whatever’s living inside them, and then you can, like, decorate your home for the holidays in peace knowing that there’s no hidden critter in your pine cone just waiting to make your house their home. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: The DIY home pest control has surged since the pandemic. People want low-chemical solutions, and that’s why I think vinegar gets so much reach. But yeah, unfortunately it’s just not as effective as everyone thought it was. Karissa: Well, it’s good to know so we don’t waste our vinegar and our time. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Yeah. Karissa: I- I have to say, though, maybe this is bad, but I do like to use just the harsh chemicals and get them out of the way- … if they do come in the house. So I, I don’t hesitate to use the big stuff. Arielle: Yeah. It’s… You know, we appreciate your honesty here. I’m sure there are a lot of listeners who struggle with pests and are like, “Yeah, I’m just gonna obliterate.” The 7 best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs Arielle: The next solution is titled, “The seven best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs”. Grocery prices are unfortunately still high, and two university horticulture experts say there are specific vegetables that genuinely pay for themselves when you grow them at home. Most of the list made sense to me, but there’s one of them that takes three years before it really starts producing, and both experts say plant it anyway. And yeah, there are pretty good reasons, which I will get into. So first, herbs are the economic winner here. They’re among the most expensive produce per ounce at the grocery store. You usually buy more than you use, and growing them means you harvest exactly what you need when you need it. The strange one was the asparagus. It takes two to three years of establishment before you get a real harvest, so you really have to be committed to the asparagus, and also you have to like asparagus. I like asparagus, but I know a lot of people aren’t the biggest fans. But a well-maintained bed produces for up to 20 years. One expert calls it something you’ll have basically for life. Both experts are clear that the garden only saves money if you plant what your household actually eats. So start with vegetables you already go through the most, and that will help you save money in the end. How EV fleets are shielding Europe from oil price volatility Arielle: The last solution that we are gonna share with everyone this week is titled “How EV fleets are shielding Europe from oil price volatility”. So there is that conflict in Iran that has been driving oil prices up 33% this year. But six European countries collectively avoided nearly $2.2 billion in oil import costs just because they have enough EVs on the road. That’s not a projection or a goal, that’s an actual number from a six-month window. Denmark alone displaced 13% of its entire 2025 oil consumption. So there’s a real dollar security argument for EV adoption here that goes beyond anything to do with the environment, although the environment is very important. Karissa: Yes. Arielle: Hopefully this, uh, this will encourage other economies to really invest in their EV development, but also hopefully this conflict ends soon. Karissa: Yeah. So- For multiple reasons, of course. But it just goes to show how moving towards renewable energy, sustainable energy across the board is just the best path towards energy security. Arielle: Definitely. Well, those were all of the solutions we had this week, but before we go, we have a positive quote. Karissa: This week we have, “Part of being optimistic is keeping one’s head pointed toward the sun, one’s feet moving forward.” And that’s from Nelson Mandela. Arielle: Beautiful. Well, everyone, I hope you enjoy your Halloween weekend if you’re celebrating, and if not, then I hope you enjoy the, uh, candy sales that are inevitably- going to happen after Halloween is over. We will both be back next week with more solutions. Karissa: Until then, have a great weekend. The post Podcast Transcript October 30th, 2026— Kenya’s wildlife deal, Halloween tips across the ages, and EV energy security first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.titleOriginal: What’s the fairest way to tax a hamburger?
items.description: Τα τρόφιμα ευθύνονται για το ένα τρίτο των εκπομπών του θερμοκηπίου της ανθρωπότητας. Και σίγουρα, τα τρόφιμα που εκπέμπουν περισσότερο άνθρακα είναι επίσης αυτά που τείνουν να είναι τα χειρότερα για την υγεία μας, όπως τα κρέατα και τα γαλακτοκομικά. Τι θα γινόταν, λοιπόν, αν προσπαθούσαμε να φορολογήσουμε αυτόν τον άνθρακα, να ωθήσουμε τους ανθρώπους σε δίαιτες υψηλότερων φυτών που είναι πιο υγιεινές για τους ανθρώπους και τον πλανήτη; Μια νέα μελέτη στο Nature Food…
items.descriptionOriginal: Food accounts for a third of humanity’s greenhouse emissions. And sure enough, the most carbon-gushing foods are also the ones that tend to be the worst for our health, such as meats and dairy. So what if we tried taxing that carbon, to nudge people toward higher-plant diets that are healthier for people and planet alike? A new study in Nature Food explores how these food emissions taxes could be applied to countries around the world with different levels of wealth and greenhouse emissions. It shows how they could be tweaked to manage the delicate interplay between food prices, poverty, hunger, and health—while still cutting billions of tons of annual emissions. Economists have estimated that growing populations and increasing meat consumption worldwide could cause the environmental footprint of our food—including greenhouse emissions— to balloon by 50 to 90 percent by 2050 . This has spurred recommendations that humanity shift its diet , toward fewer animals and more plants. Emissions taxes paid by consumers buying foods are one way to encourage a shift away from meats, dairy, eggs , and sugars . But questions remain about how those taxes can be applied fairly to countries around the world—given that wealthier nations have more ability to pay them, and that many of these same nations also contributed disproportionately to rising greenhouse gases in the first place. In the new study, researchers used economic, trade, and public health models to predict how well different types of taxes would curb greenhouse emissions—and also, how they would impact food prices climate policy of all? They compared two tax scenarios. In one, emissions are priced the same worldwide, at a constant cost of USD$ 185 per metric ton of CO 2 equivalent (tCO 2 eq). In this system, wealthy countries would still pay more taxes, because their food systems emit more tons of CO 2 . In the other system, the cost-per-ton of emissions is scaled up or down, based on each country’s wealth—thereby further increasing the taxes paid by consumers in wealthy countries (to as much as $969 per tCO 2 eq), while reducing those paid by lower-wealth countries (to as little as $21 per tCO 2 eq). The researchers compared these two scenarios both with and without a second provision, in which governments would also subsidize fruits and vegetables to further lower the prices that consumers pay for these low-carbon foods. Their results suggest that taxes based on a fixed-price-per-ton would reduce food-related emissions most sharply—by up to 18.7 percent, or about 2.6 billion tCO 2 eq worldwide each year. But such taxes would likely worsen overall health in some countries such as India, Bangladesh, and Vietnam—even after accounting for reductions in heart disease and diabetes—because they might make food less affordable to some people, compromising nutrition. The authors found that adjusting the price-per-ton of emissions based on national wealth would lessen this problem. And subsidizing the cost of fruits and vegetables would further decrease it. Together these two tweaks slightly reduced the emissions that were prevented—but they were still predicted to cut worldwide food emissions by 17 percent, or about 2.3 billion tCO 2 eq per year. The authors recommended that these efforts to reduce the negative impacts on the poor could be further explored, with detailed studies of poverty in individual countries, and potentially by excluding some critical sustenance foods such as fish or rice from the taxes in some countries. Bouyssou, et al. “ Food emissions taxes can deliver health and environmental benefits with limited leakage .” Nature Food , 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Generates Clean Energy, Saves Land, Improves Fishing—What’s Not to Like? Reading Time: 2 minutes In September 2026, solar developer D3 Energy installed a large solar array, not on land or on a rooftop, but on the surface of a reservoir that serves the water needs of the village of Monroeville, Ohio. This floating power plant covers 12 acres of the reservoir’s 16 acres. If a solar facility of this size, which contains 9,220 solar panels, were built on dry land, it would require 30 acres. So doing it the Monroeville way helps to keep open land available for farming, housing, business or industry, conservation land, or any other use. This 6-megawatt installation is projected to generate about 7,500 megawatt-hours of clean electricity to this village of 1,300 residents. Monroeville has already operated a 4-megawatt ground-mounted solar array, built in 2017. This 10-megawatt total gives the town roughly 13 times as much solar-generated power per capita as the rest of Ohio. Their floating solar array is among the five largest in the U.S. In addition to the clean power produced and the avoidance of using land that might be put toward other needed uses, Floato-voltaics projects such as this one have several other benefits. First, the physical barrier created by the floating platforms significantly reduces water evaporation by blocking direct solar radiation and intercepting wind blowing across the water’s surface. Solar “on the water” thereby reduces evaporation by 30% to 80%, depending on temperatures and humidity in the immediate area. The result, depending upon the size of the floating power plant, is an annual savings of millions of gallons of valuable drinking and irrigation water. Beyond clean power, floating solar arrays like Monroeville’s reduce reservoir water evaporation by 30% to 80% by blocking direct solar radiation and wind, saving millions of gallons of drinking and irrigation water annually. Photo courtesy of D3 Energy . Second, by depriving the water of sunlight, there is a sizable reduction of toxic algal blooms. Photosynthetic organisms like blue-green algae require sunlight to thrive. By heavily shading parts of the reservoir, the concentrations of floating solar panels limit the light penetration needed for massive algal blooms. This naturally improves water quality, reducing expenses from chemical treatments needed to purify the water. Third, more fish. During the warmer months, the floating platforms insulate the reservoir’s water against seasonal temperature spikes, helping support cold-water fish species. Local reservoirs are often favorite local fishing spots. And fourth, cleaning issues. Land-based solar arrays, whether in farming or more urbanized areas, often deal with dust, dirt, and other airborne debris. For best panel performance, cleaning of their surfaces in these situations is advisable. Open bodies of water are inherently less affected by blowing dirt and dust, keeping the panels cleaner longer and reducing maintenance costs. All things considered, with all the bodies of fresh water dotting the planet, maybe we should all look more closely for floato-voltaic opportunities just beyond our own backyard. The post Generates Clean Energy, Saves Land, Improves Fishing—What’s Not to Like? appeared first on Happy Eco News .
